name: Myofascial Pain Syndrome
pinyin: jī jīn mó téng tòng zōng hé zhēng
preview_text: In TCM, the character of your muscle pain-whether it's a deep, cold ache, a burning knot, or a stabbing trigger point-reveals the underlying pattern driving it. Most people see sig...
conventional_description:
Myofascial Pain Syndrome (MPS) is a chronic pain disorder characterized by sensitive, tight bands of muscle fiber called trigger points. These points can cause local pain or refer pain to other areas of the body, along with stiffness, weakness, and limited range of motion. It commonly affects the neck, shoulders, and back, and is often linked to repetitive strain, poor posture, or stress.
Diagnosis is made through a physical exam where a practitioner palpates for taut bands and reproduces the characteristic pain. There is no single lab test or imaging study that confirms MPS, which is why it is sometimes overlooked or mistaken for other conditions.
conventional_treatments: Standard care usually includes physical therapy, stretching exercises, and trigger point release techniques such as massage or dry needling. Trigger point injections with local anesthetics or corticosteroids are sometimes used. Medications may include NSAIDs, muscle relaxants, and occasionally low-dose antidepressants or anticonvulsants for chronic pain. Lifestyle modifications and stress management are also recommended.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, Myofascial Pain Syndrome is understood as a form of Painful Obstruction (Bi Syndrome), where the smooth flow of Qi and Blood through the muscles and fascia is blocked. The Liver plays a central role because it governs the sinews and ensures the free flow of Qi. When emotional stress, frustration, or tension disrupts the Liver, Qi stagnates and muscles tighten, creating that familiar achy, distending pain.
External pathogens like Wind, Cold, and Dampness can also invade the body's channels, especially when your defenses are low. Cold congeals the flow, causing deep, fixed pain that worsens with cold weather. Dampness creates heaviness and stiffness. Over time, unresolved stagnation can deepen into Blood Stasis-the blood thickens and congeals right inside the muscle fibers, forming the hard, stabbing knots we know as trigger points.
In some cases, the pain has a burning, swollen quality, reflecting a combination of Dampness and Heat clogging the channels. For others, especially older adults or those with chronic illness, the root is a deficiency of the Liver and Kidneys. When these organs are depleted, they cannot properly nourish the sinews and bones, leading to dull, lingering pain and weakness that never fully resolves.
Because the same Western diagnosis can stem from such different TCM patterns, treatment must be personalized. A person whose pain feels better with warmth and worse in damp weather needs a very different strategy than someone whose knots burn and feel better with cold. By reading the subtle clues in your pain, your tongue, and your pulse, a TCM practitioner can identify the pattern and design a treatment that addresses both the local trigger point and the whole-body imbalance that created it.
classical_quote: 「风寒湿三气杂至，合而为痹也。」
classical_translation: "The three Qi of Wind, Cold, and Dampness arrive together, combining to form Bi syndrome."

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by asking how the pain feels, where it is, and what makes it better or worse. They also look at your overall state - your energy, mood, and any other symptoms - because myofascial pain can arise from several different underlying imbalances. The tongue and pulse give crucial clues that help separate one pattern from another.
If the pain is a deep, heavy ache that worsens with cold or damp weather and eases with warmth, and you feel stiff and chilly, the pattern is likely Painful Obstruction with Wind-Cold-Damp. The tongue often has a thin white coating, and the pulse feels tight or wiry, reflecting an invasion of external pathogens that have lodged in the channels.
When the pain is sharp, fixed in one spot, and feels like a knife, especially when pressing on a taut band or knot, Blood Stagnation is the main pattern. The tongue may appear purplish or show dark spots, and the pulse is often choppy. This pattern often develops when earlier obstructions were not fully resolved, leading to persistent trigger points.
If the pain has a distending, moving quality and flares up with stress, frustration, or emotional upset, Qi and Blood Stagnation is at play. You might also notice chest tightness or sighing. The tongue can be dusky, and the pulse wiry. Here the liver’s role in smoothing the flow of Qi has been disrupted, causing pain that mirrors the emotional state.
When the painful area feels hot, looks slightly red or swollen, and the pain is burning rather than dull, Painful Obstruction due to Damp Heat in Channels is present. The tongue is red with a yellow coating, and the pulse is rapid. This less common pattern often appears after an injury or when dampness lingers and transforms into heat.
In chronic, nagging cases where pain is worse at night, accompanied by weakness, soreness in the low back and knees, and a sense of depletion, the root is Painful Obstruction with Liver and Kidney Deficiency. The tongue is pale with a thin coat, and the pulse is thin and weak. This pattern is more frequent in older adults or after long illness, reflecting an inability to properly nourish the sinews.

patterns.worse_with: Cold, damp, or rainy weather, Sitting in drafts or air conditioning, Cold, raw foods and icy drinks, Prolonged sitting or inactivity, Emotional stress, frustration, or worry
patterns.better_with: Applying warmth or warm compresses, Gentle stretching and movement, Dry, warm weather, Warm, cooked meals, Wearing layers to avoid drafts
patterns.why_this_happens: Wind, Cold, and Dampness are external pathogens that invade the body when your defenses are low, often after exposure to drafts, cold weather, or damp conditions. They settle into the muscles and fascia, where Cold contracts and congeals the flow of Qi and Blood, while Dampness creates a heavy, sticky stagnation. This combination leads to the tight, ropey bands and tender trigger points that define myofascial pain, with stiffness and aching that feel much worse in cold or wet weather.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, slightly swollen body with teeth marks, white greasy coating, moist surface. Pulse: wiry and tight, or soggy and slow if Dampness predominates.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Wind, Cold, and Dampness are the root cause of this pattern, so anything that introduces more cold or moisture into the body-like cold weather, drafts, or raw foods-will further congeal Qi and Blood, intensifying pain and stiffness. Warmth and gentle movement do the opposite: they disperse Cold, evaporate Dampness, and encourage a smooth flow of Qi and Blood through the affected channels, which relaxes the taut bands and relieves the trigger points.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the painful areas warm with scarves, wraps, or heat packs, and avoid sitting in drafts or air conditioning. Choose warm, cooked foods like soups and stews, and use warming spices such as ginger, cinnamon, and black pepper. Gentle daily movement like stretching or walking helps prevent stagnation, but avoid overexertion.

patterns.why_this_happens: When muscle injury, chronic tension, or unresolved pathogenic factors persist, the local circulation of Qi and Blood becomes blocked. Over time, this stagnation deepens into Blood Stasis-the blood thickens and congeals right inside the muscle fibers, forming hard, knotty trigger points that feel like palpable lumps. The pain is sharp and fixed, like a knife, because the stagnant blood presses on the nerves, and it worsens at night when the body's Yin energy naturally thickens the blood further.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: purple or dusky body with stasis spots, distended dark sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: choppy (涩 sè) like a knife scraping bamboo, or wiry (弦 xián) if Qi stagnation is involved.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Stress and frustration cause Liver Qi to stagnate, which then leads to Blood stasis-the very root of this pattern. Cold congeals blood, so cold weather and inactivity slow circulation and worsen the fixed, stabbing pain. Heat and gentle movement, on the other hand, invigorate Blood and help dissolve the knots. Warming spices like turmeric and ginger move Blood, while deep breathing encourages Qi to flow, breaking the cycle of stagnation.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid cold, raw foods and icy drinks, which congeal blood and make stasis worse. Eat warming, blood-moving foods like turmeric, ginger, hawthorn berries, black fungus, and lightly cooked greens. Gentle daily movement-such as walking, tai chi, or stretching-keeps Qi and Blood flowing. Apply a warm compress or heating pad to painful knots, and avoid sitting in one position for too long.

patterns.why_this_happens: When emotional stress or frustration disrupts the Liver’s ability to keep Qi flowing smoothly, that stagnant Qi creates a sensation of distending, tight pain in the muscles. patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress directly tightens the Liver Qi, which is the root of this pattern, so frustration or suppressed anger immediately worsens the distending pain. Cold and inactivity, on the other hand, cause further congealing and stagnation, making the pain more fixed and intense.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Incorporate gentle, rhythmic movement like walking, tai chi, or stretching to keep Qi and Blood flowing. Avoid prolonged sitting and take breaks to move. patterns.why_this_happens: Dampness and Heat combine to clog the channels that run through your muscles and fascia. This creates a hot, heavy obstruction that makes trigger points feel burning and swollen, rather than just stiff. patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, possibly slightly swollen, with a yellow greasy coating. Pulse: slippery (滑 huá) and rapid (数 shuò).

patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and deep-fried foods that create more Heat and Dampness. Favor cooling, light foods like cucumber, watermelon, mung beans, and barley. patterns.why_this_happens:
When the Liver and Kidneys become depleted-often from aging, chronic illness, or overwork-they can no longer nourish the sinews and bones. This leaves the muscles and fascia undernourished, causing dull, lingering pain and weakness.
Because the body's underlying strength is weak, it cannot properly expel external pathogens like cold and dampness, which settle into the channels and make trigger points stubborn and slow to heal.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, thin body with a thin white coating. Pulse: fine, weak, and slow, especially weak in the rear (Kidney) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold and dampness further deplete the body's warming Yang Qi and congeal Blood, making the already undernourished sinews stiffer and more painful. Rest and warmth conserve and support the deficient Kidney Yang, while gentle movement promotes Qi flow without exhausting the reserves. Warm, nourishing foods and moxibustion directly supplement the Liver and Kidneys, helping to rebuild the foundation that keeps muscles and fascia supple.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Favor warm, cooked, and easily digestible foods like bone broths, stews, and congees. Include moderate amounts of kidney-nourishing foods such as black beans, walnuts, and goji berries. Keep the body warm, especially the lower back and knees, and avoid exposure to cold and damp environments. Gentle exercises like tai chi or qigong help circulate Qi and Blood without depleting your reserves.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture really release my trigger points?
faqs.answer: Yes. Acupuncture targets both local Ashi points (the painful knots themselves) and distal points along the affected channels. The needle can elicit a brief local twitch response, which helps release the taut muscle band and restore normal blood flow. Many patients feel immediate, though sometimes temporary, relief after a session.

faqs.question: How many acupuncture sessions will I need?
faqs.answer: Most patients begin with weekly sessions for 4-6 weeks. The exact number depends on your pattern and how long you've had the pain. Acute cases may resolve in 2-4 visits, while chronic, stubborn trigger points often require 10-12 sessions or more. Your practitioner will reassess regularly and adjust the frequency as you improve.

faqs.question: Can I combine TCM with my physical therapy or medication?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. TCM works well alongside physical therapy, massage, and conventional medications. Acupuncture and herbs can enhance the effects of stretching and strengthening exercises. However, always inform both your TCM practitioner and your doctor about all treatments you are receiving, especially if you are taking blood-thinning medications or muscle relaxants.

faqs.question: Will I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Basic dietary adjustments can support your recovery. In general, avoid cold and raw foods that constrict the channels. Warm, cooked meals and spices like turmeric and ginger help move Qi and Blood. If your pattern involves Dampness, you may be asked to reduce dairy, greasy foods, and sugar. Your practitioner will give you specific guidance based on your pattern.

faqs.question: Is it normal to feel sore after acupuncture?
faqs.answer: Mild soreness or a bruised sensation at the needle sites is common, especially when trigger points are needled directly. This usually fades within a day and is a sign that the muscle is releasing. It should not be severe or debilitating. Applying a warm compress can help.

faqs.question: Can TCM help if I've had myofascial pain for years?
faqs.answer: Yes, but it requires patience. Long-standing pain often involves deeper Blood Stagnation or underlying deficiency. While some relief may come quickly, fully softening old knots and correcting the root imbalance can take several months of consistent treatment. The goal is not just temporary relief but lasting change in how your muscles hold tension.

research.title: Moxibustion therapy on myofascial pain syndrome: An evidence-based clinical practice guideline
research.description: This guideline systematically reviewed the evidence for moxibustion in treating myofascial pain syndrome. The panel found that moxibustion can significantly reduce pain intensity and improve physical function compared to conventional therapies, with a good safety profile. The recommendation was conditional due to the moderate quality of included studies.
research.periodical: Wang X, et al. Moxibustion therapy on myofascial pain syndrome: An evidence-based clinical practice guideline. Medicine. 2020;99(46):e23142.

research.title: Effect of different needling manipulations on myofascial pain syndrome: A randomized controlled trial
research.description: This trial compared different acupuncture needling techniques (lifting-thrusting vs. twirling) for myofascial pain syndrome. Both techniques reduced pain and improved local blood flow, but the combination of manipulations tailored to the TCM pattern diagnosis showed superior results in relieving trigger point sensitivity and restoring muscle function.
research.periodical: Chen L, et al. Effect of different needling manipulations on myofascial pain syndrome: a randomized controlled trial. Zhen Ci Yan Jiu. 2024;49(12):1246-1252.
